stem: A 15-year-old who uses cannabis regularly says, "It might make people feel weird on the night, but it doesn't cause real longer-term mental health problems." Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: The main ongoing concern with cannabis is appetite change rather than mental health
Mental health follow-up is only needed if there has already been an acute panic attack
Early-onset cannabis use is linked to anxiety, depression and psychosis, so longer-term mental health effects should still be discussed
Cannabis-related mental health risk only matters during withdrawal
If he is still attending school, longer-term harms are unlikely

explanation: Early-onset cannabis use is linked to anxiety, depression and psychosis, so longer-term mental health effects should still be discussed. Counselling should address these ongoing risks rather than focusing only on acute intoxication or withdrawal.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because appetite change is not the main ongoing concern highlighted here, and it ignores the longer-term mental health risks.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because mental health follow-up is relevant even without a prior panic attack.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because early-onset cannabis use is associated with anxiety, depression and psychosis, so those longer-term effects should be discussed.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the mental health risk is not limited to withdrawal; early cannabis use is also linked to longer-term harm.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because school attendance does not rule out the mental health risks associated with early cannabis use.
